description:
== Rails-native failure investigation

Rails Error Dashboard (RED) is an open-source, self-hosted Rails engine for
investigating production exceptions without sending error data to a monitoring
vendor. It groups errors and records request context and cause chains and, when
enabled, breadcrumbs plus local and instance variables captured before Ruby
unwinds the stack.

== What it records

* Rails and Ruby runtime health on the error record, refreshed on every captured
  occurrence: Active Record pool, Puma, background jobs, GC, memory, threads,
  file descriptors and system pressure
* Built-in storm protection that progressively sheds expensive context and I/O
  during error floods while retaining useful exemplars and exact occurrence
  counts
* Copy as RSpec, curl or LLM prompt; swallowed-exception detection; LLM
  observability without prompt capture; OpenTelemetry span export
* Workflow, notifications (Slack, Email, Discord, PagerDuty, webhooks) and
  two-way issue sync with GitHub, GitLab, Codeberg and Linear
* Rails-specific operational views: jobs, database, cache, Action Cable, Active
  Storage, Rack::Attack and deprecations

== Running it

Run RED with your application's database or an isolated error database, on
PostgreSQL, MySQL/Trilogy or SQLite. The dashboard is translated into 11
languages (French native-reviewed; the rest machine-translated and awaiting
native review). A
self-hosted Sentry alternative that keeps error data in your own database. The
gem is MIT and free forever.

Supports Rails 7.0-8.1 and Ruby 3.2-4.0. Beta: APIs may change before 1.0.

Live demo: https://rails-error-dashboard.anjan.dev

Documentation: https://AnjanJ.github.io/rails_error_dashboard
summary: Rails-native, self-hosted error monitoring with exception-time Ruby state, runtime health, and storm-safe capture.

description: Most Rails cookie banners ask for consent and then load Google Analytics anyway. Consently is the other half: declare your tags once - GA4, Google Tag Manager, Google Ads, Microsoft Clarity, Meta Pixel, Hotjar, Plausible or anything custom - and it renders every non-essential one as an inert script the browser will not even fetch, then turns them into live scripts the instant the visitor agrees, with no page reload. Embedded YouTube, Vimeo and Google Maps iframes wait behind a placeholder of the same size and appear on consent too, because an iframe sets cookies with no script of yours. Google Consent Mode v2 defaults are emitted before any Google tag and updated on the click, in basic mode or in advanced mode where Google's own tags load denied so Ads can model refused conversions. GA4 ecommerce events are built from your own line items rather than by hand. The banner and its preferences panel ship translated into ten European languages, styled in plain CSS with no Tailwind and no build step. Your cookie policy page is generated from the same configuration - every vendor, every cookie it sets and for how long - so it cannot drift out of date. Multi-tenant applications get per-domain or per-shop tag sets from a single initializer, one consent can span subdomains, and an optional consent log stores proof of each decision in your own database, with no third-party service and nothing leaving your infrastructure.
summary: GDPR cookie consent for Rails that actually blocks your analytics tags until the visitor agrees

description:
Ruby binding for sghtmltopdf, a successor to wkhtmltopdf: an HTML-to-PDF
rendering engine written in Rust that needs no browser process. The engine
runs in-process through a native extension and releases the GVL while
rendering. On Rails it registers a wicked_pdf compatible renderer, so
`render pdf: "invoice"` works with the keys you already use.
summary: HTML to PDF renderer that does not depend on Chromium, WebKit, or Gecko

1.0 parser with full XPath 1.0 and SAX support. The C DOM is the single
source of truth; Ruby objects are thin FFI wrappers (one Ruby method =
one FFI call).
summary: Nokogiri-compatible Ruby binding for libleptris (XML 1.0, XPath 1.0, SAX)

description:
BreakerMachines is a production-ready circuit breaker implementation for Ruby that prevents
cascade failures in distributed systems. Built on the battle-tested state_machines gem, it
provides a clean DSL, thread-safe operations, multiple storage backends, and comprehensive
introspection tools. Unlike other solutions, BreakerMachines prioritizes safety by avoiding
dangerous forceful timeouts while supporting fallback chains, jitter, and event callbacks.
summary: Circuit breaker implementation for Ruby with a clean DSL and state_machines under the hood

description:
BehaviorMachines runs behavior trees whose nodes follow the behavior-tree pattern: Sequence,
Fallback, their reactive variants, thresholded Parallel,
IfThenElse, WhileDoElse, and the usual decorators. Every running leaf the tree abandons is halted
exactly once, in the same call, so leaves can own real resources. Pure Ruby, with an optional
native backend built on the behavior-machines Rust crate, and leaves for state_machines objects.
summary: Behavior trees with explicit halt semantics, following the behavior-tree pattern

description:
RedisQueuedLocks (aka RQL, aka RQL-lock) - distributed locks with
"prioritized lock acquisition queue" capabilities based on the Redis Database.

Each lock request is put into the request queue
(each lock is hosted by its own queue separately from other queues)
and processed in order of their priority: requests of a higher priority go first,
requests of the same priority are processed in FIFO order.
Each lock request lives some period of time (RTTL) (with requeue capabilities)
which guarantees the request queue will never be stacked.

In addition to the classic queued (FIFO) strategy RQL supports random (RANDOM)
lock obtaining strategy when any acquirer from the lock queue
can obtain the lock regardless the position in the queue.

Supports lock request prioritization, Read/Write locks and Reentrant locks.

Provides flexible invocation flow, parametrized limits (lock request ttl, lock ttl,
queue ttl, lock attempts limit, fast failing, etc), zombie locks elimination,
lock indexing, logging and instrumentation (and much more).
summary: Distributed locks with "prioritized lock acquisition queue" capabilities based on the Redis Database.

description: API reference for Zernio. Authenticate with a Bearer API key. Base URL: https://zernio.com/api  Versioning and deprecation: all endpoints are versioned in the URL path (current version: /v1). Breaking changes only ship in a new path version; existing versions keep working. Deprecated operations are marked 'deprecated: true' in this spec and announced in the changelog (https://zernio.com/changelog) before removal.  Errors: every 4xx/5xx response is application/json with a machine-readable 'code' and a human-readable 'error' message (see the ErrorResponse schema).  Request ids: responses carry an X-Request-Id header with the id we log the request under. Quote it when reporting a problem. A valid x-request-id you send is reused as that id.
summary: Zernio API Ruby Gem

description:
RedisQueuedLocks (aka RQL, aka RQL-lock) - distributed locks with
"prioritized lock acquisition queue" capabilities based on the Redis Database.

Each lock request is put into the request queue
(each lock is hosted by its own queue separately from other queues)
and processed in order of their priority: requests of a higher priority go first,
requests of the same priority are processed in FIFO order.
Each lock request lives some period of time (RTTL) (with requeue capabilities)
which guarantees the request queue will never be stacked.

In addition to the classic queued (FIFO) strategy RQL supports random (RANDOM)
lock obtaining strategy when any acquirer from the lock queue
can obtain the lock regardless the position in the queue.

Supports lock request prioritization, Read/Write locks and Reentrant locks.

Provides flexible invocation flow, parametrized limits (lock request ttl, lock ttl,
queue ttl, lock attempts limit, fast failing, etc), zombie locks elimination,
lock indexing, logging and instrumentation (and much more).
summary: Distributed locks with "prioritized lock acquisition queue" capabilities based on the Redis Database.

description: Squishling makes Ruby classes elastic. Add a squishling to a class and it can send inputs straight to an LLM (OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, or any provider RubyLLM supports, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, or your own adapter) and return strict-schema-validated, typed results: the same type your Ruby code returns. Use it to gracefully maintain fickle integrations, build interfaces for unknown data formats, and rescue production errors by handing the failing call to the LLM with the source class as context. Write Ruby only for the paths where token costs justify maintaining it. Per-input routing, validated retries, and fallbacks for your LLM calls included.
summary: Elastic Ruby classes with LLM batteries included: zero-code integrations, graceful error rescue, and code only where it's worth maintaining.

description: API reference for Zernio. Authenticate with a Bearer API key. Base URL: https://zernio.com/api  Versioning and deprecation: all endpoints are versioned in the URL path (current version: /v1). Breaking changes only ship in a new path version; existing versions keep working. Deprecated operations are marked 'deprecated: true' in this spec and announced in the changelog (https://zernio.com/changelog) before removal.  Errors: every 4xx/5xx response is application/json with a machine-readable 'code' and a human-readable 'error' message (see the ErrorResponse schema).  Request ids: responses carry an X-Request-Id header with the id we log the request under. Quote it when reporting a problem. A valid x-request-id you send is reused as that id.
summary: Zernio API Ruby Gem

description:
RespondoGrpc standardizes the responses your gRPC services send. Every rpc can
return one protobuf envelope (respondo.v1.Response: success, message, data,
errors, meta), built from the same expressive helpers as its siblings
(render_grpc_ok, render_grpc_not_found, render_grpc_unprocessable, ...).
Failures finish the call with the matching gRPC status code (NOT_FOUND,
INVALID_ARGUMENT, ...) and carry the envelope in the trailing metadata, so
clients get both a proper status and structured field errors. Protobuf messages
travel as typed payloads, hashes and ActiveRecord records as JSON-like data.
Standalone gem — it does not depend on respondo (JSON) or respondo-graphql.
summary: Consistent response envelopes for gRPC services — data, errors, meta, real status codes.

description:
Relaton is the database, registry, and cache for bibliographic references
to technical standards in the Relaton/XML bibliographic model. It provides
the Relaton::Db API, a registry that lazily loads each standards-body
flavor (ISO, IETF, NIST, IEC, …) on first use, and a file-based cache.

Every flavor ships inside this single gem — `gem install relaton` gives you
the full multi-flavor setup, with flavor code loaded on demand via autoload.
The CLI (relaton-cli) is a separate gem.
summary: Relaton: bibliographic references to technical standards — database, registry, cache, and every flavor in one gem.

description:
Rodauth is Ruby's most advanced authentication framework, designed
to work in all rack applications.  It's built using Roda and Sequel,
but it can be used as middleware in front of web applications that use
other web frameworks and database libraries.

Rodauth aims to provide strong security for password storage by
utilizing separate database accounts if possible on PostgreSQL,
MySQL, and Microsoft SQL Server.  Configuration is done via
a DSL that makes it easy to override any part of the authentication
process.

Rodauth supports typical authentication features: such as login and
logout, changing logins and passwords, and creating, verifying,
unlocking, and resetting passwords for accounts.  Rodauth also
supports many advanced authentication features:

* Secure password storage using security definer database functions
* Multiple primary multifactor authentication methods (WebAuthn and
  TOTP), as well as backup multifactor authentication methods (SMS
  and recovery codes).
* Passwordless authentication using email links and WebAuthn
  authenticators.
* Both standard HTML form and JSON API support for all features.
summary: Authentication and Account Management Framework for Rack Applications

description: API reference for Zernio. Authenticate with a Bearer API key. Deprecated operations are marked 'deprecated: true' in this spec and announced in the changelog (https://zernio.com/changelog) before removal.  Errors: every 4xx/5xx response is application/json with a machine-readable 'code' and a human-readable 'error' message (see the ErrorResponse schema).  Request ids: responses carry an X-Request-Id header with the id we log the request under. Quote it when reporting a problem. A valid x-request-id you send is reused as that id.

description:
The maintainer's half of gem_kit: one RubyGems command, `gem kit`, with
subcommands for bumping the version, writing and linting the changelog,
listing outstanding deprecations, releasing and tagging.

It keeps the promises gem_kit records. `gem kit bump` refuses to move onto
a deprecation's removal version while the old name is still in the tree,
and `gem kit release` refuses to ship a version with an unkept promise or
no changelog entry of its own.

Everything is read from the .gemspec in the working directory, so the
normal case needs no configuration at all.
summary: Versioning, changelog and deprecation gates for Ruby gems

description:
Ask an AI coding agent to move a button 10 pixels left, and watch it struggle. CSS gives it five or six different ways to control position: margin, padding, a flex order, a grid column, a transform. Nothing says which one is actually in charge on this particular page, so the agent guesses, edits the wrong one, and something else quietly shifts. It reports the change as done. The page is now broken.

QSS removes the guessing by removing the choice. Every element's position and size is one explicit number, not a tug-of-war between properties. Those numbers are written in a single unit, a "qnt" (1/1000th of the layout's own width), so the same edit holds its exact proportion at any screen size -- a phone, a laptop, a 4K display -- with no breakpoints, no media queries, and no separate rules to keep in sync. Move something once and it stays put, everywhere.

That is the whole idea, and it helps humans exactly as much as it helps agents: fewer rules to maintain, one obvious place to make a change, and layouts that stay consistent across devices by construction instead of by discipline.

QSS backs that up with two automatic auditors that catch mistakes a human reviewer might miss (a RED finding is a broken rule, ORANGE is a judgment call) and a real-browser render check, because a passing lint rule is not proof a page actually displays correctly -- only watching it render is. It ships compiled, ready-to-use CSS plus its SCSS source, works with zero JavaScript, and offers an optional JS engine for a few conveniences on top. It stays out of the way of whatever you use for colors, type and visual polish (Tailwind or anything else) -- QSS only ever owns position, size and structure.

QSS was extracted from a real Rails development tool that still runs on it today, not built as a theoretical exercise. See docs/HOWTO.md to get started and docs/DESIGN_HISTORY.md for the full story of what was tried, what broke, and why each decision landed where it did.

Status: 0.x. Expect names and APIs to change before 1.0.
summary: A CSS layout system built so AI agents (and the humans reviewing them) never have to guess

description:

floors, fixed shares, an automatic win and a hold on it; estimators for values
of several parts, pooled contrasts, hierarchical rates and a change test; and

yes/no or amount outcomes, ranked or picked by one rule from a key, given
uniforms or an RNG, with the odds of what it draws: exact for a pick among
up to 20 contenders (EXACT_PICK_MAX) and for orders and positions over up to
10 free items (EXACT_ORDER_MAX) with none barred from leading, otherwise a
seeded Monte Carlo estimate with its standard error. Every random input is
injected, so each answer can be reproduced.

description:
The maintainer's half of gem_kit: one RubyGems command, `gem kit`, with
subcommands for bumping the version, writing and linting the changelog,
listing outstanding deprecations, releasing and tagging.

It keeps the promises gem_kit records. `gem kit bump` refuses to move onto
a deprecation's removal version while the old name is still in the tree,
and `gem kit release` refuses to ship a version with an unkept promise or
no changelog entry of its own.

Everything is read from the .gemspec in the working directory, so the
normal case needs no configuration at all.
summary: Versioning, changelog and deprecation gates for Ruby gems

description: Connect brokerage accounts to your app for live positions and trading.  ## Rate limiting  Two limits apply to requests signed with your `clientId`. The stricter one wins, and exceeding either returns `429 Too Many Requests`.  - **Customer-level** — 250 requests/minute by default, scoped to your   `clientId` and applied across all endpoints. Reported in   `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining` and `X-RateLimit-Reset`. - **Account-level** — 10 requests/minute per account, scoped to   (`clientId`, `accountId`). All covered operations for one account draw on   the same bucket — reading balances and reading positions share it — and   enforcement does not depend on the HTTP method, so updating an account   consumes the same bucket as reading it. Only enforced for Personal users,   and only for integrations it has been rolled out to — it is not yet in   force for every Personal integration. It also does not apply on every   operation that documents a 429 below. Where it applies it is reported in   `X-RateLimit-Account-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Account-Remaining` and   `X-RateLimit-Account-Reset`. Do not read the absence of those headers as   proof the limit is off — some configurations omit the rate limit headers   while still enforcing the limit, so header absence tells you nothing   about your allowance.  On a 429, `X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0` means you hit the customer-level limit and `X-RateLimit-Account-Remaining: 0` means the account-level one. Wait for the corresponding `*-Reset` value (seconds) before retrying, or fall back to exponential backoff with jitter.  Not every 429 is explained by those headers. A separate per-authenticated-user limit, reported in no `X-RateLimit-*` header, covers OAuth-authenticated requests and signed requests in configurations where the customer-level limit is not in effect — on the operations that use the default throttles. A few operations override those and are governed by the customer-level limit alone. The two do not stack: a signed request governed by the customer-level limit above is not additionally subject to the per-user one. If a 429 arrives with no header at zero — or with no `X-RateLimit-*` headers at all — honour `Retry-After` and back off. Treat the remaining counts as a hint, not a guarantee that the next request will succeed.  Because the customer-level limit applies everywhere, any signed request can return 429.  **OAuth-authenticated requests are an exception.** They are not subject to the customer-level limit and do not receive `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining` or `X-RateLimit-Reset` — do not wait on those headers or design around a customer-level allowance on this path. The account-level limit still applies to them on the account-data endpoints above, reported in the `X-RateLimit-Account-*` headers. On operations using the default throttles the per-user limit above applies to them as well, so an OAuth request can be rejected while the account headers still show capacity; on the few operations that override those throttles, OAuth callers have no per-user ceiling at all. Drive retries from `Retry-After` and exponential backoff with jitter rather than from the headers.  See https://docs.snaptrade.com/docs/ratelimiting.
summary: SnapTrade Ruby Gem

Line 6 saves one as an .hlx file. This gem opens that file and hands the rig back as ordinary Ruby - the blocks in order, what each one is, and every setting - so you can read a preset, compare two, or index a library of them. No hardware needed. The file is parsed by the same Rust code that talks to the pedal itself, so it reads here exactly as it does there.

description: Privileged Access Manager (PAM) helps you on your journey towards least privilege and helps mitigate risks tied to privileged access misuse or abuse. PAM allows you to shift from always-on standing privileges towards on-demand access with just-in-time, time-bound, and approval-based access elevations. PAM allows IAM administrators to create entitlements that can grant just-in-time, temporary access to any resource scope. Requesters can explore eligible entitlements and request the access needed for their task. Approvers are notified when approvals await their decision. Streamlined workflows facilitated by using PAM can support various use cases, including emergency access for incident responders, time-boxed access for developers for critical deployment or maintenance, temporary access for operators for data ingestion and audits, JIT access to service accounts for automated tasks, and more.

description:
This is the official Ruby client for the Zizq job queue server.

Zizq is a simple, single binary, zero dependency, language agnostic job queue.

Features:

- Enqueue and process jobs across programming languages
- Persistent/journalled
- Multi-thread and/or multi-fiber
- Scheduled jobs
- Prioritized queues
- Optional ActiveJob integration
- Unique jobs
- Cron scheduling (recurring jobs)
- Job introspection and management, including `jq` filters


This client supports multi-threaded and/or multi-fiber concurrency and is very fast. The Zizq server provides everything needed. There are no separate external storage dependencies to configure such as Redis or a RDBMS.

See https://zizq.io for full details and documentation.
summary: The official Ruby client for the Zizq job queue

description: Connect brokerage accounts to your app for live positions and trading.  ## Rate limiting  Two limits apply to requests signed with your `clientId`. The stricter one wins, and exceeding either returns `429 Too Many Requests`.  - **Customer-level** — 250 requests/minute by default, scoped to your   `clientId` and applied across all endpoints. Reported in   `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining` and `X-RateLimit-Reset`. - **Account-level** — 10 requests/minute per account, scoped to   (`clientId`, `accountId`). All covered operations for one account draw on   the same bucket — reading balances and reading positions share it — and   enforcement does not depend on the HTTP method, so updating an account   consumes the same bucket as reading it. Only enforced for Personal users,   and only for integrations it has been rolled out to — it is not yet in   force for every Personal integration. It also does not apply on every   operation that documents a 429 below. Where it applies it is reported in   `X-RateLimit-Account-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Account-Remaining` and   `X-RateLimit-Account-Reset`. Do not read the absence of those headers as   proof the limit is off — some configurations omit the rate limit headers   while still enforcing the limit, so header absence tells you nothing   about your allowance.  On a 429, `X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0` means you hit the customer-level limit and `X-RateLimit-Account-Remaining: 0` means the account-level one. Wait for the corresponding `*-Reset` value (seconds) before retrying, or fall back to exponential backoff with jitter.  Not every 429 is explained by those headers. A separate per-authenticated-user limit, reported in no `X-RateLimit-*` header, covers OAuth-authenticated requests and signed requests in configurations where the customer-level limit is not in effect — on the operations that use the default throttles. A few operations override those and are governed by the customer-level limit alone. The two do not stack: a signed request governed by the customer-level limit above is not additionally subject to the per-user one. If a 429 arrives with no header at zero — or with no `X-RateLimit-*` headers at all — honour `Retry-After` and back off. Treat the remaining counts as a hint, not a guarantee that the next request will succeed.  Because the customer-level limit applies everywhere, any signed request can return 429.  **OAuth-authenticated requests are an exception.** They are not subject to the customer-level limit and do not receive `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining` or `X-RateLimit-Reset` — do not wait on those headers or design around a customer-level allowance on this path. The account-level limit still applies to them on the account-data endpoints above, reported in the `X-RateLimit-Account-*` headers. On operations using the default throttles the per-user limit above applies to them as well, so an OAuth request can be rejected while the account headers still show capacity; on the few operations that override those throttles, OAuth callers have no per-user ceiling at all. Drive retries from `Retry-After` and exponential backoff with jitter rather than from the headers.  See https://docs.snaptrade.com/docs/ratelimiting.
summary: SnapTrade Ruby Gem

description: Connect brokerage accounts to your app for live positions and trading.  ## Rate limiting  Two limits apply to requests signed with your `clientId`. The stricter one wins, and exceeding either returns `429 Too Many Requests`.  - **Customer-level** — 250 requests/minute by default, scoped to your   `clientId` and applied across all endpoints. Reported in   `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining` and `X-RateLimit-Reset`. - **Account-level** — 10 requests/minute per account, scoped to   (`clientId`, `accountId`). All covered operations for one account draw on   the same bucket — reading balances and reading positions share it — and   enforcement does not depend on the HTTP method, so updating an account   consumes the same bucket as reading it. Only enforced for Personal users,   and only for integrations it has been rolled out to — it is not yet in   force for every Personal integration. It also does not apply on every   operation that documents a 429 below. Where it applies it is reported in   `X-RateLimit-Account-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Account-Remaining` and   `X-RateLimit-Account-Reset`. Do not read the absence of those headers as   proof the limit is off — some configurations omit the rate limit headers   while still enforcing the limit, so header absence tells you nothing   about your allowance.  On a 429, `X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0` means you hit the customer-level limit and `X-RateLimit-Account-Remaining: 0` means the account-level one. Wait for the corresponding `*-Reset` value (seconds) before retrying, or fall back to exponential backoff with jitter.  Not every 429 is explained by those headers. A separate per-authenticated-user limit, reported in no `X-RateLimit-*` header, covers OAuth-authenticated requests and signed requests in configurations where the customer-level limit is not in effect — on the operations that use the default throttles. A few operations override those and are governed by the customer-level limit alone. The two do not stack: a signed request governed by the customer-level limit above is not additionally subject to the per-user one. If a 429 arrives with no header at zero — or with no `X-RateLimit-*` headers at all — honour `Retry-After` and back off. Treat the remaining counts as a hint, not a guarantee that the next request will succeed.  Because the customer-level limit applies everywhere, any signed request can return 429.  **OAuth-authenticated requests are an exception.** They are not subject to the customer-level limit and do not receive `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining` or `X-RateLimit-Reset` — do not wait on those headers or design around a customer-level allowance on this path. The account-level limit still applies to them on the account-data endpoints above, reported in the `X-RateLimit-Account-*` headers. On operations using the default throttles the per-user limit above applies to them as well, so an OAuth request can be rejected while the account headers still show capacity; on the few operations that override those throttles, OAuth callers have no per-user ceiling at all. Drive retries from `Retry-After` and exponential backoff with jitter rather than from the headers.  See https://docs.snaptrade.com/docs/ratelimiting.

description:
== Rails-native failure investigation

Rails Error Dashboard (RED) is an open-source, self-hosted Rails engine for
investigating production exceptions without sending error data to a monitoring
vendor. It groups errors and records request context and cause chains and, when
enabled, breadcrumbs plus local and instance variables captured before Ruby
unwinds the stack.

== What it records

* Rails and Ruby runtime health on the error record, refreshed on every captured
  occurrence: Active Record pool, Puma, background jobs, GC, memory, threads,
  file descriptors and system pressure
* Built-in storm protection that progressively sheds expensive context and I/O
  during error floods while retaining useful exemplars and exact occurrence
  counts
* Copy as RSpec, curl or LLM prompt; swallowed-exception detection; LLM
  observability without prompt capture; OpenTelemetry span export
* Workflow, notifications (Slack, Email, Discord, PagerDuty, webhooks) and
  two-way issue sync with GitHub, GitLab, Codeberg and Linear
* Rails-specific operational views: jobs, database, cache, Action Cable, Active
  Storage, Rack::Attack and deprecations

== Running it

Run RED with your application's database or an isolated error database, on
PostgreSQL, MySQL/Trilogy or SQLite. The dashboard is translated into 11
languages (French native-reviewed; the rest machine-translated and awaiting
native review). A
self-hosted Sentry alternative that keeps error data in your own database. The
gem is MIT and free forever.

Supports Rails 7.0-8.1 and Ruby 3.2-4.0. Beta: APIs may change before 1.0.

Live demo: https://rails-error-dashboard.anjan.dev

Documentation: https://AnjanJ.github.io/rails_error_dashboard
summary: Rails-native, self-hosted error monitoring with exception-time Ruby state, runtime health, and storm-safe capture.

description:
Relaton is the database, registry, and cache for bibliographic references
to technical standards in the Relaton/XML bibliographic model. It provides
the Relaton::Db API, a registry that lazily loads each standards-body
flavor (ISO, IETF, NIST, IEC, …) on first use, and a file-based cache.

Every flavor ships inside this single gem — `gem install relaton` gives you
the full multi-flavor setup, with flavor code loaded on demand via autoload.
The CLI (relaton-cli) is a separate gem.
summary: Relaton: bibliographic references to technical standards — database, registry, cache, and every flavor in one gem.

yes/no or amount outcomes, ranked or picked by one rule from a key, given
uniforms or an RNG, with the odds of what it draws: exact for a pick among
up to 20 contenders (EXACT_PICK_MAX) and for orders and positions over up to
10 free items (EXACT_ORDER_MAX) with none barred from leading, otherwise a
seeded Monte Carlo estimate with its standard error. Every random input is
injected, so each answer can be reproduced.

description: Connect brokerage accounts to your app for live positions and trading.  ## Rate limiting  Two limits apply to requests signed with your `clientId`. The stricter one wins, and exceeding either returns `429 Too Many Requests`.  - **Customer-level** — 250 requests/minute by default, scoped to your   `clientId` and applied across all endpoints. Reported in   `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining` and `X-RateLimit-Reset`. - **Account-level** — 10 requests/minute per account, scoped to   (`clientId`, `accountId`). All covered operations for one account draw on   the same bucket — reading balances and reading positions share it — and   enforcement does not depend on the HTTP method, so updating an account   consumes the same bucket as reading it. Only enforced for Personal users,   and only for integrations it has been rolled out to — it is not yet in   force for every Personal integration. It also does not apply on every   operation that documents a 429 below. Where it applies it is reported in   `X-RateLimit-Account-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Account-Remaining` and   `X-RateLimit-Account-Reset`. Do not read the absence of those headers as   proof the limit is off — some configurations omit the rate limit headers   while still enforcing the limit, so header absence tells you nothing   about your allowance.  On a 429, `X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0` means you hit the customer-level limit and `X-RateLimit-Account-Remaining: 0` means the account-level one. Wait for the corresponding `*-Reset` value (seconds) before retrying, or fall back to exponential backoff with jitter.  Not every 429 is explained by those headers. A separate per-authenticated-user limit, reported in no `X-RateLimit-*` header, covers OAuth-authenticated requests and signed requests in configurations where the customer-level limit is not in effect — on the operations that use the default throttles. A few operations override those and are governed by the customer-level limit alone. The two do not stack: a signed request governed by the customer-level limit above is not additionally subject to the per-user one. If a 429 arrives with no header at zero — or with no `X-RateLimit-*` headers at all — honour `Retry-After` and back off. Treat the remaining counts as a hint, not a guarantee that the next request will succeed.  Because the customer-level limit applies everywhere, any signed request can return 429.  **OAuth-authenticated requests are an exception.** They are not subject to the customer-level limit and do not receive `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining` or `X-RateLimit-Reset` — do not wait on those headers or design around a customer-level allowance on this path. The account-level limit still applies to them on the account-data endpoints above, reported in the `X-RateLimit-Account-*` headers. On operations using the default throttles the per-user limit above applies to them as well, so an OAuth request can be rejected while the account headers still show capacity; on the few operations that override those throttles, OAuth callers have no per-user ceiling at all. Drive retries from `Retry-After` and exponential backoff with jitter rather than from the headers.  See https://docs.snaptrade.com/docs/ratelimiting.

description: Connect brokerage accounts to your app for live positions and trading.  ## Rate limiting  Two limits apply to requests signed with your `clientId`. The stricter one wins, and exceeding either returns `429 Too Many Requests`.  - **Customer-level** — 250 requests/minute by default, scoped to your   `clientId` and applied across all endpoints. Reported in   `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining` and `X-RateLimit-Reset`. - **Account-level** — 10 requests/minute per account, scoped to   (`clientId`, `accountId`). All covered operations for one account draw on   the same bucket — reading balances and reading positions share it — and   enforcement does not depend on the HTTP method, so updating an account   consumes the same bucket as reading it. Only enforced for Personal users,   and only for integrations it has been rolled out to — it is not yet in   force for every Personal integration. It also does not apply on every   operation that documents a 429 below. Where it applies it is reported in   `X-RateLimit-Account-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Account-Remaining` and   `X-RateLimit-Account-Reset`. Do not read the absence of those headers as   proof the limit is off — some configurations omit the rate limit headers   while still enforcing the limit, so header absence tells you nothing   about your allowance.  On a 429, `X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0` means you hit the customer-level limit and `X-RateLimit-Account-Remaining: 0` means the account-level one. Wait for the corresponding `*-Reset` value (seconds) before retrying, or fall back to exponential backoff with jitter.  Not every 429 is explained by those headers. A separate per-authenticated-user limit, reported in no `X-RateLimit-*` header, covers OAuth-authenticated requests and signed requests in configurations where the customer-level limit is not in effect — on the operations that use the default throttles. A few operations override those and are governed by the customer-level limit alone. The two do not stack: a signed request governed by the customer-level limit above is not additionally subject to the per-user one. If a 429 arrives with no header at zero — or with no `X-RateLimit-*` headers at all — honour `Retry-After` and back off. Treat the remaining counts as a hint, not a guarantee that the next request will succeed.  Because the customer-level limit applies everywhere, any signed request can return 429.  **OAuth-authenticated requests are an exception.** They are not subject to the customer-level limit and do not receive `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining` or `X-RateLimit-Reset` — do not wait on those headers or design around a customer-level allowance on this path. The account-level limit still applies to them on the account-data endpoints above, reported in the `X-RateLimit-Account-*` headers. On operations using the default throttles the per-user limit above applies to them as well, so an OAuth request can be rejected while the account headers still show capacity; on the few operations that override those throttles, OAuth callers have no per-user ceiling at all. Drive retries from `Retry-After` and exponential backoff with jitter rather than from the headers.  See https://docs.snaptrade.com/docs/ratelimiting.

description:
minitest provides a complete suite of testing facilities supporting
TDD, BDD, and benchmarking.

    "I had a class with Jim Weirich on testing last week and we were
     allowed to choose our testing frameworks. Kirk Haines and I were
     paired up and we cracked open the code for a few test
     frameworks...

     I MUST say that minitest is *very* readable / understandable
     compared to the 'other two' options we looked at. Nicely done and
     thank you for helping us keep our mental sanity."

    -- Wayne E. Seguin

minitest/test is a small and incredibly fast unit testing framework.
It provides a rich set of assertions to make your tests clean and
readable.

minitest/spec is a functionally complete spec engine. It hooks onto
minitest/test and seamlessly bridges test assertions over to spec
expectations.

minitest/benchmark is an awesome way to assert the performance of your
algorithms in a repeatable manner. Now you can assert that your newb
co-worker doesn't replace your linear algorithm with an exponential
one!

minitest/pride shows pride in testing and adds coloring to your test
output. I guess it is an example of how to write IO pipes too. :P

minitest/test is meant to have a clean implementation for language
implementors that need a minimal set of methods to bootstrap a working
test suite. For example, there is no magic involved for test-case
discovery.

    "Again, I can't praise enough the idea of a testing/specing
     framework that I can actually read in full in one sitting!"

    -- Piotr Szotkowski

Comparing to rspec:

    rspec is a testing DSL. minitest is ruby.

    -- Adam Hawkins, "Bow Before MiniTest"

minitest doesn't reinvent anything that ruby already provides, like:
classes, modules, inheritance, methods. This means you only have to
learn ruby to use minitest and all of your regular OO practices like
extract-method refactorings still apply.

== Features/Problems:

* minitest/autorun - the easy and explicit way to run all your tests.
* minitest/test - a very fast, simple, and clean test system.
* minitest/spec - a very fast, simple, and clean spec system.
* minitest/benchmark - an awesome way to assert your algorithm's performance.
* minitest/pride - show your pride in testing!
* minitest/test_task - a full-featured and clean rake task generator.
* Incredibly small and fast runner, but no bells and whistles.
* Written by squishy human beings. Software can never be perfect. We will all eventually die.
summary: minitest provides a complete suite of testing facilities supporting TDD, BDD, and benchmarking

description: Duel runs your benchmarks on two versions of your code side by side, the baseline (where your branch left main, say) and the candidate, and fails if the candidate is slower at any of them. description:
Build Bitcoin Lightning payments into your Ruby application with OpenReceive.
Work with exact money amounts, normalize wallet responses, and apply consistent
settlement rules while keeping control of your wallet and application.

This lightweight core provides money conversion, exchange rates, Nostr Wallet
Connect (NWC) adapters, and swap-address validation without a database dependency.
For a complete Rails integration, install openreceive-rails. For a custom Ruby
or Rack integration, use openreceive-server.

OpenReceive integrations support optional swaps from USDT, USDC, SOL, and ETH
through a configured provider, settling as BTC over Lightning into your wallet.
Available assets and networks depend on the provider.
summary: Bitcoin Lightning payment primitives for Ruby and Rails, plus USDT and USDC through optional swaps. Your app, your wallet.

description:
Accept Bitcoin Lightning payments directly into a wallet you control, from your
Ruby or Rack application. OpenReceive provides invoice creation, payment checks,
and settlement reconciliation through a receive-only Nostr Wallet Connect
(NWC) client. Optional swaps let customers pay with USDT, USDC, SOL, and ETH
through a configured provider; you receive BTC over Lightning in your wallet.
Available assets and networks depend on the provider.

Bring your own wallet client, authorization, and payment persistence. The service
and Rack handler fit into your existing application, with no separate OpenReceive
service or database to deploy. Your app keeps control of orders, prices, and
fulfillment; wallet credentials stay on the server. Rails developers can use
openreceive-rails for built-in payment storage and reconciliation.
summary: Accept Bitcoin Lightning payments in Ruby and Rack, plus USDT and USDC through optional swaps. Your app, your wallet.

description:
Add Bitcoin Lightning checkout to your Rails app and receive payments directly
into a wallet you control. Mount the engine, connect a receive-only Nostr Wallet
Connect (NWC) wallet, and wire up three hooks for authorization, order amounts,
and fulfillment.

Optional swaps let customers pay with USDT, USDC, SOL, and ETH through a
configured provider; you receive BTC over Lightning in your wallet. Available
assets and networks depend on the provider.

OpenReceive handles invoices, payment attempts, and settlement reconciliation
using your existing application database. Keep your orders,
users, prices, and fulfillment in your app, with no separate OpenReceive database,
Redis, or payment service to deploy. Includes an install generator, PostgreSQL,
SQLite, and MySQL support, plus an optional wallet-notifications worker.
summary: Accept Bitcoin Lightning payments in Rails, plus USDT and USDC through optional swaps. Your app, your wallet.

description:
AIA runs large language models from the terminal. Prompts are Markdown files with YAML front matter: parameters
that AIA asks for, directives such as /include and /shell, ERB and shell expansion, and keys that pick the model,
temperature or a special mode. Run a prompt once, chain prompts into a pipeline, make a prompt file executable,
or open an interactive chat with history, checkpoints and skills.

Every session is a crew of robots built on robot_lab. Name several models to compare them side by side, ask for a
consensus or a debate, have two independent answers reconciled with /verify, or decompose and delegate work to
specialists. Robots use RubyLLM tools and MCP servers through ruby_llm 2.1's built-in client, with per-tool
approval and automatic tool filtering. Any provider RubyLLM registers can be used, local or remote, plus optional
ruby_llm-providers-* gems that run Claude Code, Codex or GitHub Copilot as models. Requires Ruby 4.0.9 or newer.
summary: Command-line AI assistant: Markdown prompts with directives, ERB and shell, chat with crews of robots, MCP servers, and any RubyLLM provider including coding-agent CLIs.

description:
== Rails-native failure investigation

Rails Error Dashboard (RED) is an open-source, self-hosted Rails engine for
investigating production exceptions without sending error data to a monitoring
vendor. It groups errors and records request context and cause chains and, when
enabled, breadcrumbs plus local and instance variables captured before Ruby
unwinds the stack.

== What it records

* Rails and Ruby runtime health on the error record, refreshed on every captured
  occurrence: Active Record pool, Puma, background jobs, GC, memory, threads,
  file descriptors and system pressure
* Built-in storm protection that progressively sheds expensive context and I/O
  during error floods while retaining useful exemplars and exact occurrence
  counts
* Copy as RSpec, curl or LLM prompt; swallowed-exception detection; LLM
  observability without prompt capture; OpenTelemetry span export
* Workflow, notifications (Slack, Email, Discord, PagerDuty, webhooks) and
  two-way issue sync with GitHub, GitLab, Codeberg and Linear
* Rails-specific operational views: jobs, database, cache, Action Cable, Active
  Storage, Rack::Attack and deprecations

== Running it

Run RED with your application's database or an isolated error database, on
PostgreSQL, MySQL/Trilogy or SQLite. The dashboard is translated into 11
languages (French native-reviewed; the rest machine-translated and awaiting
native review). A
self-hosted Sentry alternative that keeps error data in your own database. The
gem is MIT and free forever.

Supports Rails 7.2-8.1 and Ruby 3.3-4.0.

Live demo: https://rails-error-dashboard.anjan.dev

Documentation: https://AnjanJ.github.io/rails_error_dashboard
summary: Rails-native, self-hosted error monitoring with exception-time Ruby state, runtime health, and storm-safe capture.

description:
Trapline sets traps for vulnerable code: it takes you from a CVE to a tested
opengrep/semgrep rule.

The web editor validates the rule YAML as you type, runs it against test code
and highlights each finding. You mark which lines must or must not match by
clicking the margin or accepting results, and Trapline writes the ruleid/ok
annotations for you, so the test file stays in the standard --test format
that opengrep and semgrep read.

Give it a CVE or GHSA id and it looks the advisory up in NVD and OSV, then
drafts rules with test code: a template for the vulnerability class (CWE), a
check for vulnerable runtime images (PHP, Python, Node.js, Ruby, Go, .NET) in
Dockerfiles, Compose, Kubernetes, Helm and CI files, a rule that finds usage
of the affected package, and a taint skeleton for 14 languages. Notes explain
what was inferred and what still needs review.

The CLI validates rules, runs their tests in CI and generates drafts. It runs
standalone (trapline server), as a Rack app or mounted in Rails, with no
runtime dependencies besides Ruby and the opengrep or semgrep binary.
summary: Write, test and generate opengrep/semgrep rules: web editor, CLI and CVE-to-rule drafts

description:
ractor-rails-shim makes a Rails application Ractor-safe, so it can run in
Ractor mode — serving requests from worker Ractors that share one frozen
app graph, instead of forking N separate processes.

Rails keeps global state (Rails.application, Rails.cache, Rails.logger,
and every config value set via mattr_accessor / class_attribute) in
class-level instance variables, which Ruby forbids reading or writing from
a non-main Ractor. The shim reroutes those accessors through Ractor-safe
storage (ActiveSupport::IsolatedExecutionState, or Ractor.store_if_absent)
and patches the handful of raw class-ivar accessors Rails reads
per-request.

It is verified against a real Rails 8.1 app (Devise, Propshaft, Kaminari,
PostgreSQL) served by the kino web server in `kino -m ractor` mode.

This is a stopgap: once Rails supports Ractor mode upstream, this gem
becomes a no-op and can be removed.
summary: Make Rails apps Ractor-safe so they can run in Ractor mode (e.g. under the kino web server).

description:
Trapline is a web editor and CLI for writing and testing opengrep/semgrep
rules, plus a generator that turns a CVE into rule drafts with test code.
Test files stay in the standard --test format.

INSTALL

  gem install trapline

Trapline needs an engine on your PATH, opengrep (recommended) or semgrep:

  curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/opengrep/opengrep/main/install.sh | bash
  pip install semgrep

The opengrep installer puts the binary in ~/.opengrep/cli/latest/. Add it to
your PATH or pass --engine-bin. Check the setup with:

  trapline version

USAGE

Web editor (http://127.0.0.1:9292):

  trapline server -r ./rules

Write the rule, paste vulnerable and fixed code, and click the margin to mark
the lines that must or must not match. Trapline writes the ruleid/ok
annotations and reruns as you type.

Rule drafts from a CVE or GHSA (looked up in NVD and OSV):

  trapline cve CVE-2024-4577                           # list the drafts
  trapline cve CVE-2024-4577 --save --pick 2 -r ./rules

Validate and test rules (exits 1 on failure, for CI):

  trapline validate --engine rules/*.yaml
  trapline test -r ./rules
  trapline run rules/my-rule.yaml app/models/user.rb

Rails: add gem "trapline" to the Gemfile, then

  bin/rails generate trapline:install    # editor at /trapline
  bin/rails trapline:test

It also runs as a Rack app (run Trapline::Web::App.new in config.ru). No
runtime dependencies besides Ruby 3.3+ and the engine binary.
summary: Write, test and generate opengrep/semgrep rules: web editor, CLI and CVE-to-rule drafts
requirements:
---
- opengrep or semgrep on PATH to run rules

description:
RedisQueuedLocks (aka RQL, aka RQL-lock) - distributed locks with
"prioritized lock acquisition queue" capabilities based on the Redis Database.

Each lock request is put into the request queue
(each lock is hosted by its own queue separately from other queues)
and processed in order of their priority: requests of a higher priority go first,
requests of the same priority are processed in FIFO order.
Each lock request lives some period of time (RTTL) (with requeue capabilities)
which guarantees the request queue will never be stacked.

In addition to the classic queued (FIFO) strategy RQL supports random (RANDOM)
lock obtaining strategy when any acquirer from the lock queue
can obtain the lock regardless the position in the queue.

Supports lock request prioritization, Read/Write locks and Reentrant locks.

Provides flexible invocation flow, parametrized limits (lock request ttl, lock ttl,
queue ttl, lock attempts limit, fast failing, etc), zombie locks elimination,
lock indexing, logging and instrumentation (and much more).
summary: Distributed locks with "prioritized lock acquisition queue" capabilities based on the Redis Database.

description: Duel runs your benchmarks on two versions of your code side by side, the baseline (where your branch left main, say) and the candidate, and fails if the candidate is slower at any of them. Timings are judged by a distribution-free confidence interval for paired CPU-time ratios and confirmed in fresh processes, so it fails on real regressions, not noise.
summary: Performance regression guards: fail when a change makes your code slower

description:
A production-grade Ruby client for Nostr Wallet Connect (NIP-47). Handles the Nostr
protocol, NIP-04 and NIP-44 v2 encryption, secp256k1 key derivation, Schnorr signing,
and — most importantly — a reliable long-running WebSocket connection to the relay
with heartbeat pings, forced recycle, exponential backoff, and SIGTERM handling.
Developers call `pay_invoice`, `make_invoice`, `lookup_invoice`, etc. and
`subscribe_to_notifications { |n| ... }` — the transport reliability is hidden.
summary: Ruby client for Nostr Wallet Connect (NIP-47) with safe long-running relay connections.

description:
Mammoth Data Plane is the open-source PostgreSQL change-event delivery
runtime in the Mammoth ecosystem.

It realizes the CDC Ecosystem pgoutput and cdc-core libraries for PostgreSQL,
then delivers normalized changes to webhook endpoints with durable
checkpointing, retry state, dead letters, and operational visibility.

Mammoth Data Plane is application-first: it can be installed as a Ruby gem,
packaged into a container image, or deployed into Kubernetes with Helm.
summary: Mammoth Data Plane for reliable PostgreSQL change-event delivery.

description: Connect brokerage accounts to your app for live positions and trading.  ## Rate limiting  Two limits apply to requests signed with your `clientId`. The stricter one wins, and exceeding either returns `429 Too Many Requests`.  - **Customer-level** — 250 requests/minute by default, scoped to your   `clientId` and applied across all endpoints. Reported in   `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining` and `X-RateLimit-Reset`. - **Account-level** — 10 requests/minute per account, scoped to   (`clientId`, `accountId`). All covered operations for one account draw on   the same bucket — reading balances and reading positions share it — and   enforcement does not depend on the HTTP method, so updating an account   consumes the same bucket as reading it. Only enforced for Personal users,   and only for integrations it has been rolled out to — it is not yet in   force for every Personal integration. It also does not apply on every   operation that documents a 429 below. Where it applies it is reported in   `X-RateLimit-Account-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Account-Remaining` and   `X-RateLimit-Account-Reset`. Do not read the absence of those headers as   proof the limit is off — some configurations omit the rate limit headers   while still enforcing the limit, so header absence tells you nothing   about your allowance.  On a 429, `X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0` means you hit the customer-level limit and `X-RateLimit-Account-Remaining: 0` means the account-level one. Wait for the corresponding `*-Reset` value (seconds) before retrying, or fall back to exponential backoff with jitter.  Not every 429 is explained by those headers. A separate per-authenticated-user limit, reported in no `X-RateLimit-*` header, covers OAuth-authenticated requests and signed requests in configurations where the customer-level limit is not in effect — on the operations that use the default throttles. A few operations override those and are governed by the customer-level limit alone. The two do not stack: a signed request governed by the customer-level limit above is not additionally subject to the per-user one. If a 429 arrives with no header at zero — or with no `X-RateLimit-*` headers at all — honour `Retry-After` and back off. Treat the remaining counts as a hint, not a guarantee that the next request will succeed.  Because the customer-level limit applies everywhere, any signed request can return 429.  **OAuth-authenticated requests are an exception.** They are not subject to the customer-level limit and do not receive `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining` or `X-RateLimit-Reset` — do not wait on those headers or design around a customer-level allowance on this path. The account-level limit still applies to them on the account-data endpoints above, reported in the `X-RateLimit-Account-*` headers. On operations using the default throttles the per-user limit above applies to them as well, so an OAuth request can be rejected while the account headers still show capacity; on the few operations that override those throttles, OAuth callers have no per-user ceiling at all. Drive retries from `Retry-After` and exponential backoff with jitter rather than from the headers.  See https://docs.snaptrade.com/docs/ratelimiting.
summary: SnapTrade Ruby Gem

description:
Build Bitcoin Lightning payments into your Ruby application with OpenReceive.
Work with exact money amounts, normalize wallet responses, and apply consistent
settlement rules while keeping control of your wallet and application.

This lightweight core provides money conversion, exchange rates, Nostr Wallet
Connect (NWC) adapters, and swap-address validation without a database dependency.
For a complete Rails integration, install openreceive-rails. For a custom Ruby
or Rack integration, use openreceive-server.

OpenReceive integrations support optional swaps from USDT, USDC, SOL, and ETH
through a configured provider, settling as BTC over Lightning into your wallet.
Available assets and networks depend on the provider.
summary: Bitcoin Lightning payment primitives for Ruby and Rails, plus USDT and USDC through optional swaps. Your app, your wallet.

description:
Accept Bitcoin Lightning payments directly into a wallet you control, from your
Ruby or Rack application. OpenReceive provides invoice creation, payment checks,
and settlement reconciliation through a receive-only Nostr Wallet Connect
(NWC) client. Optional swaps let customers pay with USDT, USDC, SOL, and ETH
through a configured provider; you receive BTC over Lightning in your wallet.
Available assets and networks depend on the provider.

Bring your own wallet client, authorization, and payment persistence. The service
and Rack handler fit into your existing application, with no separate OpenReceive
service or database to deploy. Your app keeps control of orders, prices, and
fulfillment; wallet credentials stay on the server. Rails developers can use
openreceive-rails for built-in payment storage and reconciliation.
summary: Accept Bitcoin Lightning payments in Ruby and Rack, plus USDT and USDC through optional swaps. Your app, your wallet.

description:
Add Bitcoin Lightning checkout to your Rails app and receive payments directly
into a wallet you control. Mount the engine, connect a receive-only Nostr Wallet
Connect (NWC) wallet, and wire up three hooks for authorization, order amounts,
and fulfillment.

Optional swaps let customers pay with USDT, USDC, SOL, and ETH through a
configured provider; you receive BTC over Lightning in your wallet. Available
assets and networks depend on the provider.

OpenReceive handles invoices, payment attempts, and settlement reconciliation
using your existing application database. Keep your orders,
users, prices, and fulfillment in your app, with no separate OpenReceive database,
Redis, or payment service to deploy. Includes an install generator, PostgreSQL,
SQLite, and MySQL support, plus an optional wallet-notifications worker.
summary: Accept Bitcoin Lightning payments in Rails, plus USDT and USDC through optional swaps. Your app, your wallet.

description:
BreakerMachines is a production-ready circuit breaker implementation for Ruby that prevents
cascade failures in distributed systems. Built on the battle-tested state_machines gem, it
provides a clean DSL, thread-safe operations, multiple storage backends, and comprehensive
introspection tools. Unlike other solutions, BreakerMachines prioritizes safety by avoiding
dangerous forceful timeouts while supporting fallback chains, jitter, and event callbacks.
summary: Circuit breaker implementation for Ruby with a clean DSL and state_machines under the hood

description:
BehaviorMachines runs behavior trees whose nodes follow the behavior-tree pattern: Sequence,
Fallback, their reactive variants, thresholded Parallel,
IfThenElse, WhileDoElse, and the usual decorators. Every running leaf the tree abandons is halted
exactly once, in the same call, so leaves can own real resources. Pure Ruby, with an optional
native backend built on the behavior-machines Rust crate, and leaves for state_machines objects.
summary: Behavior trees with explicit halt semantics, following the behavior-tree pattern

description: ChronoMachines offers a flexible and configurable solution for handling transient failures in distributed Ruby applications. It provides powerful retry strategies, including exponential backoff and full jitter, with customizable callbacks. Features optional Rust-powered native performance on CRuby with pure Ruby fallback for JRuby compatibility.
summary: A robust Ruby gem for implementing retry mechanisms with exponential backoff and jitter.

description: A monotonic deadline token that derives child budgets, cancels down its tree, and raises only at checkpoints you choose. The shared time contract for the machines family: retries, circuit breakers and throttles read one budget instead of each keeping its own clock.
summary: Deadline propagation and cooperative cancellation for Ruby

description: A flat finite state machine answers which state comes next. This answers what happens to the states it was inside of: the least common ancestor of a source and a target, the exit set innermost first, the entry set outermost first, parallel regions and history. Bound to Ruby from the no_std harel-machines crate: the tree algebra only, with events, guards and callbacks left to state_machines.
summary: Statechart hierarchy for Ruby: which states a transition exits and enters

description: HyperLogLog, Count-Min Sketch, t-digest, cuckoo filter and Space-Saving top-k, bound to Ruby from the no_std probabilistic-machines crate. Each sketch answers a counting question in memory fixed at construction time, and serialises to a byte string other languages reading the same crate can decode.
summary: Distinct counts, quantiles and frequencies in bounded memory

description: Fault injection for chaos engineering: arms a named experiment that makes a dependency fail, stall or lie for a share of calls, so the breakers, retries and budgets around it can be shown to work. Bound to Ruby from the zero-dependency rogue-machines crate. Disarmed by default, and every experiment carries an expiry it cannot outlive.
summary: Fault injection and chaos engineering for Ruby

description: A supervision tree that restarts what died the way OTP would: one_for_one, one_for_all or rest_for_one, bounded by a restart intensity that escalates instead of thrashing. The decisions come from the no_std supervisor-machines crate; Ruby owns the threads, the restart backoff comes from chrono_machines and the shutdown budget from deadline_machines.
summary: OTP-style supervision trees over Ruby threads

description: ThrottleMachines provides ultra-thin, elegant rate limiting with temporal precision for distributed systems.
summary: Advanced Rate limiting for Ruby applications

description:
BreakerMachines is a production-ready circuit breaker implementation for Ruby that prevents
cascade failures in distributed systems. Built on the battle-tested state_machines gem, it
provides a clean DSL, thread-safe operations, multiple storage backends, and comprehensive
introspection tools. Unlike other solutions, BreakerMachines prioritizes safety by avoiding
dangerous forceful timeouts while supporting fallback chains, jitter, and event callbacks.
summary: Circuit breaker implementation for Ruby with a clean DSL and state_machines under the hood

description:
BehaviorMachines runs behavior trees whose nodes follow the behavior-tree pattern: Sequence,
Fallback, their reactive variants, thresholded Parallel,
IfThenElse, WhileDoElse, and the usual decorators. Every running leaf the tree abandons is halted
exactly once, in the same call, so leaves can own real resources. Pure Ruby, with an optional
native backend built on the behavior-machines Rust crate, and leaves for state_machines objects.
summary: Behavior trees with explicit halt semantics, following the behavior-tree pattern

description: ChronoMachines offers a flexible and configurable solution for handling transient failures in distributed Ruby applications. It provides powerful retry strategies, including exponential backoff and full jitter, with customizable callbacks. Features optional Rust-powered native performance on CRuby with pure Ruby fallback for JRuby compatibility.
summary: A robust Ruby gem for implementing retry mechanisms with exponential backoff and jitter.

description: A flat finite state machine answers which state comes next. This answers what happens to the states it was inside of: the least common ancestor of a source and a target, the exit set innermost first, the entry set outermost first, parallel regions and history. Bound to Ruby from the no_std harel-machines crate: the tree algebra only, with events, guards and callbacks left to state_machines.
summary: Statechart hierarchy for Ruby: which states a transition exits and enters

description: HyperLogLog, Count-Min Sketch, t-digest, cuckoo filter and Space-Saving top-k, bound to Ruby from the no_std probabilistic-machines crate. Each sketch answers a counting question in memory fixed at construction time, and serialises to a byte string other languages reading the same crate can decode.
summary: Distinct counts, quantiles and frequencies in bounded memory

description: Fault injection for chaos engineering: arms a named experiment that makes a dependency fail, stall or lie for a share of calls, so the breakers, retries and budgets around it can be shown to work. summary: Fault injection and chaos engineering for Ruby

description:
Principles helps teams keep an agent's operating guidance consistent as their harness evolves.
Name a principle and map the instruction passages, rules, skills, agents, hooks and checks that carry it.
The principles CLI reports changed or broken members and guides the agent through assessing the whole set,
fixing problems or recording open findings, and keeping the map and audit history in version control.

The CLI tracks state and validates references deterministically; the consuming agent supplies the judgement.
It calls no model and never edits the project's guidance. Structured results provide the next command,
evidence requirements and repairs. Context-loading information helps the agent assess unnecessary guidance.
The gem provides a host-independent command-line runtime for Ruby 3.4.x with no runtime gem dependencies.
summary: Maps and audits agent guidance to catch harness drift and debt

description: Duel runs your benchmarks on two versions of your code side by side, the baseline (where your branch left main, say) and the candidate, and fails if the candidate is slower at any of them. Timings are judged by a distribution-free confidence interval for paired CPU-time ratios and confirmed in fresh processes, so it fails on real regressions, not noise.
summary: Performance regression guards: fail when a change makes your code slower

description: A Duel plugin: each worker gets a MySQL server of its own, and every benchmark is judged on the statements it sent, the rows they read and their time too.
summary: A MySQL server for each Duel worker, and what it did for each benchmark

description: A Duel plugin: every benchmark is judged on the SQL queries, cached queries, transactions and record instantiations Active Record did for it too, whatever the database.
summary: What Active Record did for each Duel benchmark: queries, transactions and records

description: A Duel plugin: benchmarks with threads of their own are judged on how long their threads waited for the GVL too, so a change that adds contention fails even when its CPU time doesn't.
summary: How long threads waited for the GVL, for every Duel benchmark with threads of its own

description: A Duel plugin for Rails apps: each version of the app booted like production, with its own bundle and database, and benchmarks of its requests, judged on time, allocations, queries, views and cache use.
summary: Performance regression guards for Rails apps, with Duel

description: A Duel plugin: each worker gets a memcached server of its own, and every benchmark is judged on the memcached operations, misses and bytes it took too.
summary: A memcached server for each Duel worker, and what it did for each benchmark

description: A Duel plugin: each worker gets a PostgreSQL server of its own, and every benchmark is judged on the queries it sent, the rows they returned, the buffers they touched and their time too.
summary: A PostgreSQL server for each Duel worker, and what it did for each benchmark

description: A Duel plugin: every benchmark is judged on the Ruby objects its iterations leave alive after a full garbage collection, so a leak, or a cache that grows with every call, fails.
summary: What each Duel benchmark leaves alive: objects that outlive the garbage collector

description: A Duel plugin: each worker gets a Redis server of its own, and every benchmark is judged on the Redis CPU time, commands and round trips it took too.
summary: A Redis server for each Duel worker, and what it did for each benchmark

description: The Ruby AI framework. Build AI features the Ruby way, with conventions that feel at home in Rails: switch models without rewriting your code, then grow from a single call to production agents that run code in a sandbox, follow skills, and resume across jobs. Features chat (text, images, audio, PDFs), tools, MCP, structured output, evaluations, embeddings, image, audio, and video generation, Rails integration, and streaming. Works with OpenAI, Azure, Anthropic, Google Gemini, Vertex AI, AWS Bedrock, xAI, Cohere, DeepSeek, Mistral, Perplexity, OpenRouter, ElevenLabs, Deepgram, Ollama and GPUStack (local models), and any OpenAI-compatible API. Plain Ruby with a small set of runtime dependencies.

description:
Build Bitcoin Lightning payments into your Ruby application with OpenReceive.
Work with exact money amounts, normalize wallet responses, and apply consistent
settlement rules while keeping control of your wallet and application.

This lightweight core provides money conversion, exchange rates, Nostr Wallet
Connect (NWC) adapters, and swap-address validation without a database dependency.
For a complete Rails integration, install openreceive-rails. For a custom Ruby
or Rack integration, use openreceive-server.

OpenReceive integrations support optional swaps from USDT, USDC, SOL, and ETH
through a configured provider, settling as BTC over Lightning into your wallet.
Available assets and networks depend on the provider.
summary: Bitcoin Lightning payment primitives for Ruby and Rails, plus USDT and USDC through optional swaps. Your app, your wallet.

description:
Accept Bitcoin Lightning payments directly into a wallet you control, from your
Ruby or Rack application. OpenReceive provides invoice creation, payment checks,
and settlement reconciliation through a receive-only Nostr Wallet Connect
(NWC) client. Optional swaps let customers pay with USDT, USDC, SOL, and ETH
through a configured provider; you receive BTC over Lightning in your wallet.
Available assets and networks depend on the provider.

Bring your own wallet client, authorization, and payment persistence. The service
and Rack handler fit into your existing application, with no separate OpenReceive
service or database to deploy. Your app keeps control of orders, prices, and
fulfillment; wallet credentials stay on the server. Rails developers can use
openreceive-rails for built-in payment storage and reconciliation.
summary: Accept Bitcoin Lightning payments in Ruby and Rack, plus USDT and USDC through optional swaps. Your app, your wallet.

description:

Optional swaps let customers pay with USDT, USDC, SOL, and ETH through a
configured provider; you receive BTC over Lightning in your wallet. Available
assets and networks depend on the provider.

OpenReceive handles invoices, payment attempts, and settlement reconciliation
using your existing application database. Keep your orders,
users, prices, and fulfillment in your app, with no separate OpenReceive database,
Redis, or payment service to deploy. Includes an install generator, PostgreSQL,
SQLite, and MySQL support, plus an optional wallet-notifications worker.
summary: Accept Bitcoin Lightning payments in Rails, plus USDT and USDC through optional swaps. Your app, your wallet.

description:
Relaton is the database, registry, and cache for bibliographic references
to technical standards in the Relaton/XML bibliographic model. It provides
the Relaton::Db API, a registry that lazily loads each standards-body
flavor (ISO, IETF, NIST, IEC, …) on first use, and a file-based cache.

Every flavor ships inside this single gem — `gem install relaton` gives you
the full multi-flavor setup, with flavor code loaded on demand via autoload.
The CLI (relaton-cli) is a separate gem.
summary: Relaton: bibliographic references to technical standards — database, registry, cache, and every flavor in one gem.

description:
# Banco

Summarise bank statement CSV files from the command line.

## Installation

```sh
gem install banco
```

Requires Ruby >= 3.3.

## Usage

Navigate to the directory containing your CSV file and run:

```sh
banco
```

Banco scans for CSV files, lets you pick one (or pass `--file`), then
presents an interactive menu:

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| `a` | All transactions |
| `o` | Outgoing transactions |
| `i` | Incoming transactions |
| `m` | Money-out summary (grouped) |
| `n` | Money-in summary (grouped) |
| `b` | Bottom line (net position) |
| `s` | Save summary as CSV (prompts for path, default is `<filename>_summary.csv`) |
| `t` | Save transactions as CSV (prompts for path, default is `<filename>_transactions.csv`) |
| `l` | Load a new file |
| `+` | Merge another file into the current dataset |
| `q` | Quit |

Use `--format json` or `--format csv` for pipe-friendly output (no menu, exits after printing).

## CLI flags

| Flag | Default | Description |
|------|---------|-------------|
| `-f`, `--file FILE` | — | CSV file to analyse |
| `-F`, `--format FORMAT` | `text` | Output format: `text` / `json` / `csv` |
| `-b`, `--bank NAME` | `legacy` | Bank CSV format (see Bank formats below) |
| `-p`, `--prefix-length N` | `9` | Description prefix length for grouping |
| `-H`, `--header` | off | Skip first row as header (auto-detected when the first row is non-numeric) |
| `--from DATE` | — | Filter from date (format matches bank format) |
| `--to DATE` | — | Filter to date (format matches bank format) |
| `-v`, `--version` | — | Print version and exit |
| `-h`, `--help` | — | Show help and exit |

### Examples

```sh
# Summarise all transactions in statements.csv
banco --file statements.csv

# September only, JSON output
banco --file statements.csv --from 01/09/17 --to 30/09/17 --format json

# Skip header row, group by first 6 characters
banco --file export.csv --header --prefix-length 6
```

## Bank formats

| Name | Date format | Columns | Notes |
|------|-------------|---------|-------|
| `legacy` | `%d/%m/%y` | date, description, type, credit, debit | Default — Barclays-style, separate money-in / money-out columns |
| `split_columns` | `%d/%m/%Y` | date, description, type, credit, debit | Like `legacy` with a 4-digit year |
| `signed_amount` | `%Y-%m-%d` | date, description, amount | Single signed amount column, no type column |
| `date_description_amount` | `%d/%m/%Y` | date, description, amount, trailing | Signed amount at second-to-last position; trailing column (balance, reference, etc.) ignored. Tolerates unquoted commas in descriptions. |

### Column ordering

`date_description_amount` uses `Date | Description | Amount | trailing column`:

```
Date        Description                    Amount    Balance/Reference
07/10/2026  SAINSBURYS S/MKTS LEWES ROAD   -22.05    72.73
07/10/2026  MARLEY EI  Loan/rent           450.00    1093.70
```

The trailing column (Balance or Reference) is always ignored. The Amount column is read
from the **second-to-last** position, so unquoted commas inside a description (which
can appear in credit card exports) do not shift the Amount value.

`legacy` and `split_columns` use `Date | Description | Type | Credit | Debit`:

```
Date        Description             Type      Credit    Debit
21/09/17    Incoming Transaction    credit    12.34
21/09/17    Outgoing Transaction    Purchase            12.34
```

### Signed amount columns

When a format maps `credit_column` and `debit_column` to the **same** column
(as `signed_amount` and `date_description_amount` do), that column is read as a
single **signed** amount: positive values are money in (credit) and negative values
are money out (debit). Formats with separate columns (`legacy`, `split_columns`)
read each column directly.

### Custom formats

Define your own format in `~/.banco/formats.rb`:

```ruby
Banco::BankFormat.define(:my_bank) do
  date_column        0
  description_column 2
  type_column        1
  credit_column      3
  debit_column       4
  date_format        '%Y-%m-%d'
end
```

Then use it with `banco --bank my_bank`.

## CSV format (legacy)

Banco's default (`--bank legacy`) expects columns in this order:

| # | Content |
|---|---------|
| 1 | Date (`dd/mm/yy`) |
| 2 | Description |
| 3 | Type |
| 4 | Money in |
| 5 | Money out |

Header rows are auto-detected and skipped. Pass `--header` explicitly to suppress the warning. Any columns beyond the fifth are ignored.

## Licence

MIT — see [LICENSE](LICENSE).

Hope your numbers are positive!

description:
Flay analyzes code for structural similarities. Differences in literal
values, variable, class, method names, whitespace, programming style,
braces vs do/end, etc are all ignored. Making this totally rad.

== Features/Problems:

* Reports differences at any level of code.
* Adds a score multiplier to identical nodes.
* Differences in literal values, variable, class, and method names are ignored.
* Differences in whitespace, programming style, braces vs do/end, etc are ignored.
* Works across files.
  * Add the flay-persistent plugin to work across large/many projects.
* Run --diff to see an N-way diff of the code.
* Provides conservative (default) and --liberal pruning options.
* Provides --fuzzy duplication detection.
* Language independent: Plugin system allows other languages to be flayed.
  * Ships with .rb and .erb.
  * javascript and others will be available separately.
* Includes FlayTask for Rakefiles.
* Uses path_expander, so you can use:
  * dir_arg -- expand a directory automatically
  * @file_of_args -- persist arguments in a file
  * -path_to_subtract -- ignore intersecting subsets of files/directories
* Skips files matched via patterns in .flayignore (subset format of .gitignore).
* Totally rad.
summary: Flay analyzes code for structural similarities
